newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK government witholds report on scandal official.
newsitem.headline: HK government witholds report on scandal official.

text.p: The Hong Kong government on Wednesday refused to release internal reports shedding light on the mysterious dismissal of a top official to a legislative panel probing the case.

Secretary for the Civil Service Lam Woon-kwong, summoned to testify at the Legislative Council (Legco) inquiry's latest session, told Legco the reports on ousted former Immigration Director Laurence Leung were confidential.

Legco agreed to hold Wednesday's session behind closed doors following a request by Lam, the government's personnel chief. Earlier sessions of the Legco probe, the equivalent of a parliamentary inquiry, have been open to the press.

"Disclosing the reports would bring about the collapse of the whole (personnel) vetting system," Lam, speaking in Chinese, told the panel. "Then in the future it will be impossible for the government to carry out reliable extended vetting," he said.
"For these reasons I would say the discussion about disclosing the reports should be conducted in camera (private)," Lam said.
Lam's superior, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, who is second only to colonial Governor Chris Patten, was also set to be questioned by the panel about the confidential reports on Leung on Wednesday.
At issue are two reports -- the findings of a graft probe on Leung, and a vetting report on him aimed at assessing an official's personal integrity and honesty.
Both reports have been mentioned earlier by Lam as the basis for bundling Leung off into early retirement last year.
The Leung affair has polluted the political atmosphere in the run-up to China's recovery of sovereignty over Hong Kong, at midnight on June 30.

Leung's post was highly sensitive because he had authority over immigration, nationality and frontier affairs, as well as access to confidential information on citizens, which carries strong security implications ahead of Chinese rule.
He has denied allegations in the British press that he was a Chinese spy or that he gave Beijing sensitive information on Hong Kong residents who held British passports.
He told the inquiry earlier that the government forced him to step down for reasons unknown to him.

The government is under intense pressure to come clean on details of the case. Having initially said Leung had quit for personal reasons last July, it changed its story last week and accused Leung of serious lapses in personal integrity.
The lapses did not amount to criminal offences but made him unfit to stay in his highly sensitive job, it said.
A source close to the case said the government might be worried that some of the evidence against Leung might not stand up in court if a legal challenge to the case was mounted.

Lam, however, addressing the panel last week, said a graft probe into Leung had shown he had undisclosed business dealings, inappropriate business ties with a legislator and an investment in a Chinese enterprise, and that he had violated rules on repayment of a government housing loan.
